newsitem.title: USA: TWA 800 families to press airline for compensation.
newsitem.headline: TWA 800 families to press airline for compensation.

text.p: Families of victims of last summer's crash of TWA Flight 800 said on Saturday they will press TWA for immediate compensation.

Their announcement came after about 100 family members met with U.S. officials investigating the July 17 explosion of the Trans World Airline Boeing 747 off New York's Long Island, killing all 230 people on board.
On Friday the National Transportation Safety Board said a buildup of volatile vapors in the 747's partially full center fuel tank could have triggered the explosion.

But it stopped short of blaming the explosion of the New York-to-Paris flight on mechanical failure, a bomb or a missile, and issued urgent recommendations to the Federal Avition Administration to prevent any such future explosions.

A spokesman for the families, Jose Cremades, said a representative would meet with Trans World Airlines officials on Monday to press for funds to help families whose main wage earner was killed in the crash.
Cremades said many family members were encountering financial hardship since the crash five months ago.

He also said members agreed that claims they file for the $75,000 compensation authorized under the Warsaw Convention for deaths in international aviation would not resolve any other claims they might make.
"This does not preclude anything else," said Cremades, who lost a 15-year-old son in the crash.
Several lawsuits have already been filed claiming damages.
Cremades told a news conference the families also agreed a memorial should be built for the victims, but a place and its financing had not been decided.
"The wounds are still bleeding," he said. "The persons lost in this plane are still very present in our minds."

Asked about the meetings with the investigators from the board, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Navy, he said "the general feeling was that the briefing was worthwhile, but there was not a lot of new information."
"The key issues that we wanted to find answers to have not been answered. Maybe they cannot be answered now." he said.
Cremades said the investigators told the families they did not know whether the 747, made by Boeing Co, was brought down by mechanical failure, bomb or missile.
The board called on the FAA to issue orders to assure agaisnt vapor build up and any aircraft design changes necesary.
The FAA said it would urgently review the recommendations. Boeing said it would comply with any FAA directives issued.
TWA's New York-to-Paris flight went down shortly after takeoff. The Navy salavaged more than 90 percent of the plane's wreckage.
Cremades said the investigators told the families they had recovered about all of the center fuel tank, "but have not found any evidence of damage by a missile or a bomb."
Asked about recurring theories that it was struck by a missile shortly after takeoff, he said the investigators told them they had found no sign of a missile or bomb.
But, he said, "They are running missile tests in California."
While the board said in its report that evidence from the wreckage was "consistent" with a fuel tank explosion, it stopped short of blaming the crash on mechanical reasons.
It said the cause of the explosion was still open, but the tenor of its comments and recommendations came the closest yet to ruling out a bomb or missile attack.
However, James Kallstrom, head of the FBI's New York office, took issue with safety board speculation that static electricity caused the explosion.
He said through a spokesman it was not helpful for investigators to speculate about the cause of the crash.
An NTSB statement said parts of the wreckage pulled up from the ocean bottom showed no evidence a bomb or missile had brought the plane down.
Instead, it showed that the partially full center wing fuel tank was deformed "consistent with an explosion originating within the tank."
It said hot air from the air conditioning units just beneath the tank of Flight 800 might have heated the fuel to flash point temperatures but it was not known what actually led to ignition.
Officials said one of the immediate fixes would be to closely monitor the heat of the fuel in partially full tanks, which tends to rise faster than full tanks, or to fill the tank with an inert gas.
They said a long-term design change would be to require insulation between the tanks and heat generating units, such as the air conditioners.
